hints: Start by finding the peak of each curve in Fig. 5.1. Read across to the y-axis for activity and down to the x-axis for temperature for both ficin (x) and papain (o).
Now compare the shapes on either side of the peaks. Look at how quickly each curve rises from $20^\circ\text{C}$ to its peak, and how quickly it falls after its peak.
Look for where the two curves cross over at about $54-55^\circ\text{C}$. State clearly where papain is below ficin and where it is above, quoting temperatures and % values to support each point.
walkthrough:
Find the Optimum Temperatures**
Both curves are plotted as percentage of maximum activity, so 100% is the optimum for that enzyme. For ficin the peak is at $45^\circ\text{C}$ with 100% activity. For papain the peak is at $60^\circ\text{C}$ with 100% activity. So papain has the higher optimum temperature.

Compare Activity Below and Above the Crossover**
The curves cross at about $54-55^\circ\text{C}$ where both are about 70% activity. Between $20^\circ\text{C}$ and $54^\circ\text{C}$ papain is always lower. For example at $40^\circ\text{C}$ ficin is ~84% but papain is only ~24%. Above $55^\circ\text{C}$ papain is always higher. For example at $60^\circ\text{C}$ papain is 100% but ficin is only ~56%.

Compare the Steepness of Rise and Fall**
From $20^\circ\text{C}$ to the peak, ficin rises very steeply while papain rises more gradually. After the peak, papain falls very steeply from 100% at $60^\circ\text{C}$ to ~36% at $80^\circ\text{C}$, while ficin falls more gradually from its peak. Pick any three of these comparative points with data for full marks.

Final answer: Papain has higher optimum temperature of $60^\circ\text{C}$ compared to $45^\circ\text{C}$ for ficin; papain has lower % maximum activity than ficin from $20^\circ\text{C}$ to ~$55^\circ\text{C}$; papain has higher % maximum activity than ficin above ~$55^\circ\text{C}$ to $80^\circ\text{C}$. Papain shows slower rise to peak but steeper fall after peak than ficin.

hints: An oral drug for intestinal worms will act inside the human gut. Think about what temperature it must work at and read the two values off Fig. 5.1 at that temperature.
walkthrough:
Match Enzyme to Body Temperature**
The human intestine is at about $37^\circ\text{C}$. At $37-40^\circ\text{C}$ in Fig. 5.1, ficin is at ~75-84% of maximum activity while papain is only at ~20-24%. Ficin will therefore digest nematode proteins much faster in the body, so choose ficin and link the choice to higher activity at body temperature.
Final answer: Select ficin, as it has higher activity than papain at $37^\circ\text{C}$ (human body temperature).

hints: Think about what happens if enzyme is free in solution mixed with antibody fragments. How would you get the enzyme back out, and what would happen to your product?
walkthrough:
Why Immobilise the Enzyme**
Free ficin stays mixed with the Fab fragments, so the product is contaminated and the expensive enzyme is lost. If ficin is bound to an inert support it stays in the reactor while substrate flows past and product flows out. This means the enzyme is easily recovered and reused, is often more stable, and the Fab product is pure with no extra separation step needed.
Final answer: Immobilised ficin can be easily separated from the product and reused, and product is not contaminated with enzyme / less downstream processing needed.

hints: Recall the two words used to classify enzymes by site of action: those that act inside the cell that made them versus those secreted to act outside.
walkthrough:
Name the Location of Action**
An enzyme made inside a cell but secreted to act outside the cell is called an extracellular enzyme. Streptopain is synthesised by S. pyogenes then secreted to hydrolyse proteins in human tissue, so it fits this definition.

hints: Think about what gives skin, tendons and connective tissue its strength and elasticity. Which fibrous proteins do you know from that tissue?
walkthrough:
Recall Connective Tissue Proteins**
Human connective tissue is strengthened by tough, insoluble fibrous structural proteins. The main example is collagen, with elastin also present for elasticity. Streptopain hydrolyses these extracellular fibres to help the bacterium spread through tissue.
